799.title: Which voice speaks to you
799.hook: each reader finds one Bhagat who feels like a friend
799.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru, and some readers return again and again to particular shabads, including Bhagats' hymns, that they hold dear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Bhagat a day: a week of mornings, a different voice each one, the ang as the address. Your line was one a day. Did a note go up where your morning starts? Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

A question worth asking slowly: which of these voices would you sit next to on a long bus ride? Not which one is greatest. The Granth doesn't rank them, and neither will we. Just which one you'd want beside you. The one who asks plainly for flour and a cow. The one who dreams of a city with no sorrow in it. The one who says hard things with a grin. Some readers find, after a while, one voice they keep going back to. Today: which voice speaks to you.
screen: `A LONG BUS RIDE.` → `NOT WHO'S GREATEST.` → `WHO YOU'D SIT BESIDE.`

segments.voice: Listen to how differently they speak. Dhanna, the farmer, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, makes an arti, a hymn of worship, that reads in paraphrase like a shopping list handed to God: flour, lentils, a little ghee, shoes, good clothes, a cow, a horse. A man asking his Lord for the things a household needs, without embarrassment. Ravidas, in Raag Gauri on Ang 345, does the opposite kind of thing. He describes a city called Begampura, the place without sorrow, where there's no tax and no fear, where no one is second or third class, and he says that city is his home. Kabir, in his saloks, is the friend who tells you the truth to your face and doesn't soften it, often with a picture from the loom or the market. And Farid, in Raag Asa on Ang 488, sings of hearts dyed in love for God: his verses ache for the Beloved. Four temperaments. A farmer's frankness. A dream of a fair city. A sharp tongue. A long ache. They're all in the same book, all sung as gurbani, and none is placed above another. That's why the question isn't which one is right. It's which one you can hear. A person going through a hard month might lean toward Farid. Someone tired of a world that sorts people might lean toward Ravidas. Someone who prays best in plain words might lean toward Dhanna. Gurbani speaks of the Lord as a friend, mit or sajan. A favorite Bhagat isn't a replacement for that. It's more like a friend who shows the way to the Friend.
screen: `DHANNA ASKS FOR FLOUR AND A COW.` · `RAVIDAS DREAMS OF A CITY WITHOUT SORROW.` · `KABIR AND FARID: SHARP TONGUE, LONG ACHE.` · `NONE RANKED; WHICH ONE CAN YOU HEAR?` · then, large: `A FRIEND IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your Bhagat. In the sit, let the four voices pass by, one at a time: Dhanna's plain list, Ravidas's city, Kabir's sharp line, Farid's ache. Don't choose too fast. Just notice which one you'd want to hear again tomorrow. If none stands out, that's an answer too, and the week of reading will help. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mit. Gurbani's word for a friend: the Lord as a friend, and a favorite Bhagat as a friend who shows the way to the Friend.
Your line: a friend in the granth. Today, say the name of the Bhagat you'd sit beside, out loud once, and find one of their lines to read tonight. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: One Guru, many voices
800.hook: Sikhs honor the Bhagats' hymns as fully part of the Guru
800.howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, opening it each morning and laying it to rest each evening, and every hymn in it, the Gurus' and the Bhagats', is honored in the same way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mit: Dhanna's plain list, Ravidas's city, Kabir's edge, Farid's ache. Your line was a friend in the granth. Did a name come to you? Day eight hundred.

Someone walks into the gurdwara hall, takes off their shoes, covers their head, and walks up the aisle toward the Granth under its canopy. They kneel and touch their forehead to the floor. A small question hides in that bow. Which part of the book is it for? The Gurus' hymns? The Bhagats'? The pages of Kabir, the pages of Farid, the Var of the minstrels? Nobody bows to a chapter. The bow goes to the whole Granth at once. Today: one Guru.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED.` → `A BOW TO THE FLOOR.` → `WHICH PAGES IS IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Sikhs call the Granth the Guru Granth Sahib, and they mean Guru. Not a book about the Guru, but the Guru present, honored as a living teacher. Sikhs say Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and since then there has been no human Guru. So when Sikhs speak of the Guru today, they mean this book, all of it. Now look at how many voices are in it. The Gurus themselves wrote under one name. Their hymns carry the signature Nanak, whether the hymn is by Guru Nanak or Guru Arjan or another Guru, and a heading marked Mahala tells you which. Many hands, one name. Then the Bhagats, from different trades and towns and paths, with their own names in the headings. Then the Bhatts' swayyas, the minstrels' Var, Sundar's Sadd. Different voices from different times and places, some from Hindu backgrounds, some Muslim. And Sikhs don't treat these as layers of lesser and greater. Guru Ram Das, in Raag Nat on Ang 982, says in paraphrase that the bani is the Guru and the Guru is the bani. The word itself is the teacher. That line is the key to this whole block. If the word is the Guru, then every word in the Guru's book is the Guru's word, whoever's mouth it first came from. Kabir's line and Guru Nanak's line get the same canopy, the same chauri waved over them, the same morning opening and the same evening rest. That's what one Guru means here. Not one voice. One Guru speaking through many voices, and one bow that covers them all.
screen: `THE GRANTH IS THE GURU, PRESENT.` · `THE GURUS SIGN AS NANAK.` · `BHAGATS, BHATTS, MINSTRELS: MANY VOICES.` · `THE BANI IS THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow to the whole Granth. If you're near a gurdwara or a Granth today, you can let one bow carry all of it in mind: the Gurus, the Bhagats, the minstrels. If you're not, then for this sit, picture the whole book closed under its cloth, every voice inside it. Breathe with the picture. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. If you'd like, lower your head slightly at the end, as a small bow. The bell holds the time.
One Guru. Sikhs honor the whole Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru, the Bhagats' hymns fully part of it: many voices, one bow.
Your line: one bow covers them all. Today, when you read or hear any line from the Granth, whoever's name is in the heading, notice that Sikhs hear it as the same teacher speaking. Day eight hundred.

801.title: The Bhagats close
801.hook: the Guru's book is a house with room for saints of every kind
801.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs point to them, along with langar and the shared sangat, as the Guru's teaching that the door is open to people of every caste and faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Guru: the bani is the Guru, and one bow covers every voice in the book. Your line was one bow covers them all. Did a line from the Granth reach you as the same teacher speaking? Day eight hundred one.

A long table for a big family dinner, and the extra chairs keep coming out of the back room. A cousin's new husband. A neighbor nobody expected. The aunt who isn't speaking to the uncle, seated three chairs away from him. Somehow the table stretches. Nobody is sent home to eat alone. For a long stretch now we've been walking through a book that works like that table. Today the Bhagats close, and the question is simple: who got a chair?
screen: `A LONG FAMILY TABLE.` → `MORE CHAIRS FROM THE BACK.` → `WHO GOT A CHAIR?`

segments.voice: Look down the table. Kabir, the weaver of Benares, with his warp and weft and his sharp tongue. Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan, a Sufi, asking us to look under our own collar. Namdev, the calico printer, whose temple, tradition says, turned to face him. Ravidas, the shoemaker, whose family carried the dead cattle, dreaming of Begampura. Then the others. Trilochan and the last thought. Beni and the stages of life. Dhanna the farmer. Sain the barber. Pipa the king. Sadhna's plea for grace. Ramanand's home colored with love. Parmanand: hear, then do. Surdas's single line. Jaidev, the old poet. Bhikhan's medicine. And around them, the Bhatts with their praise, Satta and Balvand forgiven and sung, the saloks to Mardana, Sundar's call. A weaver beside a king. A Muslim saint beside a Hindu devotee. A man from a family others kept at a distance beside a Brahmin. Guru Arjan, in Raag Suhi on Ang 747, says in paraphrase that the teaching is shared by all four castes, the Khatri, the Brahmin, the Shudra and the Vaishya alike. The Bhagat pages are that line, put into practice. The Gurus didn't just say the table was open. They set the places. And here's the thing to carry out of this block: the room wasn't made by agreeing on everything. The Gurus kept voices they answered, sometimes putting the same image another way. The table holds difference without throwing anyone out. Tomorrow we turn from the book to the people. The next stretch is the people around the Gurus, starting at home, with Guru Nanak's mother and father.
screen: `WEAVER, SUFI, CALICO PRINTER, SHOEMAKER.` · `FARMER, BARBER, KING, AND MORE.` · `ONE TEACHING FOR ALL FOUR CASTES.` · `ROOM WITHOUT AGREEING ON EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `ROOM FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make room for someone. In the sit, bring to mind one person who usually ends up on the edge: of a conversation, a group chat, a family gathering. Don't fix anything yet. Just picture a chair being pulled out for them at your table. Breathe with that picture. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. After the bell, look for one real way to make that room today. The bell holds the time.
Sant. A saint or holy person: the weaver, the Sufi, the shoemaker, the farmer, the barber and the king, all honored this way at one table.
Your line: room for all. Today, pull out one chair, in a room or in a conversation, for someone who usually doesn't get one. Day eight hundred one.

802.title: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu
802.hook: Nanak's mother loved him gently; his father, an accountant, worried for his future
802.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Nanak's childhood from the janamsakhis, especially at Gurpurab, and the sacha sauda, the true bargain, is among the stories children hear at home and in gurdwara classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant: a weaver beside a king, a Sufi beside a shoemaker. Your line was room for all. Did you pull out a chair for someone? Day eight hundred two.

A father counts out coins into his son's hand. Go to the market, he says. Buy well, sell well, come home with a profit. Show me you can make your way. The son comes home with empty hands and no goods. On the road, he says, he met holy men who hadn't eaten, and he fed them. That, he says, was the true bargain. The father is furious. The mother, as tradition remembers her, is gentler. A new part of the path begins today: the people around the Gurus. And it starts at home, with Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu.
screen: `COINS FOR THE MARKET.` → `EMPTY HANDS, FED STRANGERS.` → `A NEW PART: THE PEOPLE AROUND THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: The story of the coins isn't in the Granth. It comes from the janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs remember it as the sacha sauda, the true bargain. The janamsakhis give us his parents in a few strokes. His father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts, a practical man with a practical hope: that his son would find steady work and get on in the world. His mother, Mata Tripta, the stories remember as gentle, the one who loved the boy as he was. Here's what's worth noticing. The stories don't make Mehta Kalu a villain. A father worried about money and a future is not a bad man. He's a father. In one story, the boy grows quiet and withdrawn, lying for days without wanting to eat, and the family, worried, calls in a physician. And here the Granth itself has a line. In a salok in Raag Malar, on Ang 1279, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: they called the physician to treat me; he took my arm and felt for the illness; the simple physician doesn't know the pain is deep inside, in the heart. Whether that salok was spoken in that very room, the sources don't settle. But it fits. The family's worry was real, and so was their love. They just couldn't see where the ache was. That's the picture of this home. A mother's gentleness. A father's worry. Neither of them fully understood their son, and both of them loved him. Love and worry live in the same house, at the same table, often in the same parent.
screen: `THE TRUE BARGAIN: A JANAMSAKHI STORY.` · `A FATHER WHO KEPT ACCOUNTS.` · `A PHYSICIAN WHO MISSED THE ACHE.` · `GENTLENESS AND WORRY, BOTH LOVE.` · then, large: `LOVE AND WORRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a parent's worry. In the sit, bring to mind someone who worried about you: a parent, a grandparent, a guardian, an older friend. Remember one thing they worried over, maybe something that annoyed you at the time. Then look underneath it for the love that was holding it. You don't have to agree with the worry. Just see what it was made of. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mata. A title of honor for the Gurus' mothers and wives: Guru Nanak's mother, gentle, her husband worried, and love and worry living in the same home.
Your line: love and worry. Today, if you can, tell someone who worried about you that you know it came from love, or simply say thank you for it in your own heart. Day eight hundred two.

803.title: Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram
803.hook: his sister and her husband took Nanak to Sultanpur and found him work
803.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki in the stories of Guru Nanak's life, and the tera, tera story from the Sultanpur storehouse is told to children as a lesson that everything belongs to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu: a mother's gentleness, a father's worry. Your line was love and worry. Did you find the love under someone's worry? Day eight hundred three.

Back home, things aren't going well. The young man gives away what he's meant to sell. He sits for hours with wandering holy men. His father is running out of patience. Then a message comes from another town. His older sister has married and moved away, and she and her husband have a room, and maybe a job. Come stay with us, she says. Today: Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram.
screen: `THINGS AREN'T GOING WELL AT HOME.` → `A MESSAGE FROM ANOTHER TOWN.` → `COME STAY WITH US.`

segments.voice: Bebe Nanaki was Guru Nanak's older sister. Bebe is an affectionate word for an elder sister, and Sikhs still say her name with it. In the janamsakhis, she's the one in the family who seems to see her brother clearly from the start. Where others saw a boy who wouldn't settle, the stories have her seeing something holy. She married Jai Ram, who, tradition says, worked in Sultanpur for the local governor, Daulat Khan Lodi. And here's where help becomes practical. Jai Ram used his place to find his wife's brother a job, in the modikhana, the government storehouse where grain was kept and given out. It's not a glamorous detail. It's a brother-in-law making a call. The stories say Nanak did the work honestly and well. And they tell one famous moment from that storehouse. Weighing out grain, counting each measure aloud, he came to the number tera, which in Punjabi also means yours. Tradition says he stopped counting and kept saying it: tera, tera, yours, yours, everything is Yours. It was in Sultanpur, too, in the stories, that his great turning came. But notice who got him there. Not a king or a priest. A sister who believed in him and a brother-in-law who opened a door. Family who helps doesn't always look like a sermon. Sometimes it's a spare room and an introduction.
screen: `BEBE: AN ELDER SISTER, WITH LOVE.` · `JAI RAM FINDS HIM WORK.` · `TERA, TERA: YOURS, YOURS.` · `A SPARE ROOM AND AN INTRODUCTION.` · then, large: `FAMILY WHO HELPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help a sibling. In the sit, bring to mind a brother or sister, or a cousin or friend who's close as one. Think of where they might be stuck right now. Not what's wrong with them. What door might be closed in front of them. Then ask what small door you could open: a message, a name, a ride, a room. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bebe Nanaki. Guru Nanak's older sister, who, with her husband Jai Ram, welcomed him to Sultanpur and found him work in the storehouse. Today's word.
Your line: family who helps. Today, do one practical thing for a sibling or someone close as one: a call, an introduction, a small open door. Day eight hundred three.

804.title: Mata Sulakhni
804.hook: Nanak's wife, whose steadiness made the travels possible
804.tomorrow: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth
804.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Mata Sulakhni as Guru Nanak's wife and the mother of Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das, and her place in his life is remembered in the tellings of his marriage and travels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram: a sister who believed and a brother-in-law who opened a door in Sultanpur. Your line was family who helps. Did you open a small door for someone? Day eight hundred four.

Behind a famous journey there is often someone who didn't go. Someone who kept the lamps lit, answered the door, fed the children, and was there when the traveler came back dusty from the road. The traveler gets the stories. The one at home gets a line or two, if that. Guru Nanak's long journeys are told and retold in the janamsakhis. The woman who stayed is mentioned far more briefly. Today, her name: Mata Sulakhni.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO DIDN'T GO.` → `THE TRAVELER GETS THE STORIES.` → `A LINE OR TWO FOR HOME.`

segments.voice: Start with honesty about the sources. The janamsakhis say much more about Guru Nanak's travels than about his marriage. Mata Sulakhni appears in them, but she rarely speaks. Tradition says she was the daughter of Mool Chand and that they married at Batala. Their sons were Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. Beyond that, the old stories give us her presence more than her words, and it would be wrong to fill the silence with made-up speeches. So look at what the stories do show. When Guru Nanak left on his long journeys, preaching the Name far from home, someone had to keep that home standing. The children had to be raised. The household had to run. That was Mata Sulakhni, and in some tellings the family, including Bebe Nanaki, helped her. Without that steadiness, the travels don't happen. Nobody can carry a message across many lands if the ground behind them is falling apart. And here's what's worth carrying. A great deal of faithful life looks like this. Not a sermon from a mountaintop. A pot on the stove, a child's lesson checked, a door answered, day after day, while someone else's work goes out into the world. Sikhs call her Mata, mother, as a title of honor. Steady at home isn't the small part of the story. It's the part the rest of the story stands on.
screen: `THE SOURCES SAY LITTLE.` · `SHE KEPT THE HOME STANDING.` · `THE TRAVELS STAND ON HER STEADINESS.` · `MATA: A TITLE OF HONOR.` · then, large: `STEADY AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a steady person. In the sit, bring to mind someone whose steadiness lets other people's lives move: a parent at home, a coworker who keeps things running, a friend who's always there. Picture one ordinary thing they do that nobody claps for. Hold it in mind with each breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. Later today, tell them you noticed. The bell holds the time.
Mata Sulakhni. Guru Nanak's wife, who kept the home and raised their sons while he traveled; the stories give her presence more than her words.
Your line: steady at home. Today, thank one steady person out loud, and name the ordinary thing they do. Day eight hundred four.

805.title: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth
805.hook: Guru Angad's wife is praised by name in the minstrels' Var for her generous kitchen (Ramkali, ang 967)
805.howItsDone: Gurdwaras run a langar, a free kitchen where anyone may sit and eat, and Sikhs remember Mata Khivi as one who shaped that service at Khadur Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sulakhni: the home kept standing while Guru Nanak traveled. Your line was steady at home. Did you thank someone steady? Day eight hundred five.

A huge pot of rice pudding, thick and sweet, a ladle as long as a forearm, and a line of people that doesn't end. Somebody has to decide that the pudding gets real ghee, not the cheap stuff, even though there are so many mouths. That somebody, in the Guru's house at Khadur, has a name, and the name made it into scripture. It's also the end of a week, so we'll look back too. Today: Mata Khivi.
screen: `A HUGE POT OF RICE PUDDING.` → `REAL GHEE, FOR EVERYONE.` → `A NAME IN SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Mata Khivi was the wife of Guru Angad, and Sikhs remember her as the one who ran the langar, the free kitchen, at Khadur. Some of the people in this part of the path are known to us mainly from later stories, like the janamsakhis. Mata Khivi is different. She's named in the Granth itself. Remember Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var sits in Raag Ramkali? In that Var, on Ang 967, Balvand speaks of her. In paraphrase: Khivi is a good woman, and her shade is thick and cool, like a leafy tree. In the langar, the wealth of the Word is shared out, and rice pudding made with ghee is served, sweet as nectar. Two kinds of food in one line. The Word, given freely. And kheer, rice pudding, made rich with ghee, given just as freely. Shade is the picture: people come in from the heat and rest under her care. Notice what this tells us. A woman's kitchen work is honored in the Guru's book, by name, as part of the Guru's house. The langar isn't a side room to the faith. It's where the faith gets fed to people. And the generosity is in the ghee. Feeding many people cheaply would have been easier. The line praises richness. Now the week. Which voice speaks to you. One Guru, many voices. The Bhagats close, with room for all. Then home: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu, love and worry. Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram, family who helps. Mata Sulakhni, steady at home. And today, Mata Khivi's generous kitchen.
screen: `MATA KHIVI RAN THE LANGAR.` · `NAMED IN THE VAR, ANG 967.` · `SHADE LIKE A LEAFY TREE; KHEER WITH GHEE.` · `A WEEK OF VOICES AND A HOME.` · then, large: `GENEROUS KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cook generously. In the sit, picture a meal you'll make or share this week, and picture who could eat it with you. Then picture the ghee: the one thing you could make a little richer than you have to. More of something good. A second helping set aside. A neighbor's plate. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mata Khivi. Guru Angad's wife, who ran the langar at Khadur and is praised by name in the Var of Satta and Balvand, her kitchen serving kheer made with ghee.
Your line: generous kitchen. Today, make or share one thing with more care than it strictly needs, and offer some to someone else. Day eight hundred five.

fork.setup: you're running the langar and the line of hungry people is long. ghee is expensive. what do you do?
options: use less ghee so the pudding stretches.
serve only the first part of the line.
make the kheer rich with ghee for everyone.
fork.reveal: Balvand's line praises Mata Khivi's langar for kheer made with ghee, sweet as nectar.

original.note: Gurmukhi: langar, the free kitchen of the Guru's house.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru's wife cooked for visitors.
what it means: Mata Khivi ran the langar, and her generous kitchen is honored by name as part of the Guru's house.
what a scholar hears: the Var of Satta and Balvand in Raag Ramkali names her on Ang 967, a woman of the Gurus' household praised in the Granth's own text.
